Copying Before Suppression: What Drives a Below-Chance Dip During Language Model Training?

Tejas Dahiya Affiliation: University of Chicago Email: tdahiya@uchicago.edu    Cole Blondin Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: ctblondin@gmail.com
Abstract

Mechanistic interpretability usually studies fully trained models, yet the computations that drive a behaviour can change while the model is still learning the task. On the Indirect Object Identification task, a model reads a sentence such as “When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to” and should continue with Mary, the name mentioned once, rather than John, the name mentioned twice. Pythia models pass through an early training window in which they prefer the repeated name, so accuracy in a choice between the two names falls below one half while language-model loss on a fixed text sample keeps decreasing across the same window. The window reflects a temporary imbalance between two computations. We identify one cause of the wrong preference by selecting a set of attention heads that write the repeated name, on prompts separate from those used for causal evaluation, keeping that selection fixed, and then replacing each head’s final-token output with its average output on a separate set of non-repeated-name prompts. This improves the correct-minus-repeated logit difference in a separately trained 160M model and in the official 160M, 410M, and 1B models. At 160M, the head that lowers the repeated name in the mature model shows little of its mature behaviour at this point. It directs less than one percent of its attention to the repeated mention, and its output makes almost no direct contribution to lowering that name’s logit. Both properties grow over the interval in which behaviour recovers. Across the 160M, 410M, and 1B models, transplanting the corresponding head’s mature parameters into the early checkpoint recovers 35 to 68 percent of the total improvement in the correct-minus-repeated logit difference seen by the end of training. Related early-to-late reversals appear at further Pythia scales, in two independently trained GPT-2 models, and in OLMo. A mature circuit can therefore conceal a transient causal configuration that shaped behaviour earlier in training.

1 Introduction

Much work in mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse engineer circuits, subgraphs of neural networks that implement interpretable model behaviours (Olah et al., 2020). One of the most thoroughly studied examples is indirect object identification (IOI), in which a model completes a sentence such as “When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to” with the indirect object “Mary.” In GPT-2 Small, this behaviour is implemented by a circuit containing attention heads with distinct roles, including moving candidate names toward the output and suppressing the repeated subject (Wang et al., 2023). Mechanistic analyses have identified structured computations in other settings as well, including induction heads involved in in-context learning (Olsson et al., 2022) and a circuit for numerical greater-than comparisons in GPT-2 Small (Hanna et al., 2023).

These studies show how trained models implement particular behaviours, but the mechanism visible at the end of training need not reveal how that mechanism developed. A growing line of work therefore studies model internals across training. Prior work has tracked the development of linguistic representations (Saphra and Lopez, 2019), the emergence of induction heads (Olsson et al., 2022), the gradual internal changes underlying grokking (Nanda et al., 2023), and the evolution of task circuits across training and model scale (Tigges et al., 2024). Together, these results motivate studying not only which computations are present in a trained model, but also when they emerge and how their causal roles change during training.

In this work, we study this question in IOI using the Pythia model family (Biderman et al., 2023). Across the primary Pythia scales and independently trained variants, forced-choice accuracy between the correct indirect object (IO) and the repeated subject (S) falls substantially below chance early in training before recovering. In the released Pythia models, the floor occurs within the first 3000 training steps, with performance recovering soon afterwards. For Pythia 160M, this deterioration occurs while language-model loss on a fixed sample of Pile text continues to decrease. Related early-to-late causal reversals also appear at additional model scales, in independently trained GPT-2 models, and in OLMo, although we do not assume that these settings share the same underlying circuit.

This behaviour is difficult to explain with a simple picture in which task-relevant components strengthen together and performance improves monotonically. We instead test whether the below-chance window reflects a temporary imbalance between computations that develop at different times.

Our causal experiments support this account. At the floor, a set of attention heads makes a prompt-specific contribution that increases the model’s preference for the repeated subject, and changing the identity supplied at their earlier source position redirects which name they support. Later in training, a suppressing head selected at maturity becomes strongly engaged and makes a substantial causal contribution to the correct preference. Transplanting its mature parameters into the floor model partially moves behaviour toward the mature state. We also localise an early-to-late reversal in causal role to the residual-stream state at the second subject mention. Together, these results show that a mature circuit can conceal a transient causal configuration present earlier in training, and that aggregate measures such as language-model loss can mask non-monotonic dynamics in particular behaviours.

2 Setup

Models and checkpoints.

Our main analyses use the official Pythia 160M, 410M, and 1B models (Biderman et al., 2023). Each model has 154 released checkpoints. These include the initialisation checkpoint, 10 early checkpoints spaced logarithmically through step 512, and checkpoints every 1000 steps from step 1000 to step 143000. For our main analyses, we use the 1000-step checkpoints around the below-chance window.

We also analyse a separately trained Pythia 160M model with the same architecture and tokenizer. Around the below-chance window, this model has checkpoints every 50 steps, which lets us locate the floor and recovery more precisely. We use larger Pythia models, two Stanford CRFM GPT-2 training runs (Karamcheti et al., 2021), and OLMo (Groeneveld et al., 2024) to test whether the early-to-mature reversal also appears at other model sizes and in other model families. We use PolyPythia (van der Wal et al., 2025) for a different purpose. Its independently varied training runs let us test whether the below-chance window and the floor effect recur when the random seed, data order, or parameter initialisation changes.

For each training trajectory, we call the checkpoint with the lowest forced-choice accuracy the floor. We call the last available checkpoint the mature checkpoint. The floor occurs at step 2000 for the official Pythia 160M and 410M models, step 1000 for Pythia 1B, and step 2850 for the separately trained 160M model. We define the recovery checkpoint as the first checkpoint after the floor at which forced-choice accuracy exceeds chance again, meaning accuracy is above 50%50\%. The recovery interval runs from the floor through the recovery checkpoint.

Task and notation.

We follow the standard IOI notation. Each prompt contains two single-token first names. The correct continuation, the indirect object I​OIO, appears once. The other, the subject SS, appears twice. We refer to the first and second mentions of the repeated name as S​1S1 and S​2S2, and we refer to the final sequence position, at which the model should predict IO, as E​N​DEND. For every sentence template, we permute the orders of IO and S1, so the position of a name alone does not reveal the correct answer. Figure 5 in Appendix A illustrates this notation.

Evaluation.

Our primary comparison asks which of the two task-relevant names receives the higher logit at END. We define the logit difference as

LD=ℓ⁡(I​O)−ℓ⁡(S),\mathrm{LD}=\ell(IO)-\ell(S), (1)

where ℓ⁡(⋅)\ell(\cdot) is the logit at END. A positive value means that the model prefers the correct once-mentioned name, while a negative value means that it prefers the repeated name. Forced-choice accuracy is the fraction of prompts for which LD>0\mathrm{LD}>0, whereas the reported mean logit difference averages LD\mathrm{LD} across prompts. Accuracy therefore measures how often the correct name wins, while mean logit difference measures the average magnitude and direction of the preference.

3 A Below-Chance Window

3.1 The behavioural reversal

For all three official Pythia models, the same non-monotonic pattern appears during training. Forced-choice accuracy begins near chance, falls below one half to an early minimum, and later rises to near ceiling. The logit difference follows the same reversal, becoming negative during the window in which forced-choice accuracy is below chance and positive again after recovery (Figure 1). At the 160M floor, S receives mean probability 0.02380.0238, compared with 0.01180.0118 for IO, yielding a forced-choice accuracy of 0.3170.317. The mean vocabulary ranks are 14.914.9 and 29.429.4, respectively.

The floor does not coincide with a deterioration in next-token prediction. On a fixed sample of Pile text drawn from the same corpus that Pythia was pretrained on, language-model loss for Pythia 160M falls monotonically across the checkpoints surrounding the floor, from 3.733.73 at step 1000 to 2.682.68 at step 10000. This aggregate performance improvement masks task-specific performance degradation for IOI. Additional evaluations in Appendix K show that other structured tasks follow different trajectories over the same period of training.

3.2 The window is robust across training runs and prompts

The below-chance window is not specific to one training run. We examine nine additional 160M Pythia runs from the PolyPythia collection, in which either the random seed, the order of the training data, or the parameter initialisations are changed (van der Wal et al., 2025). Forced-choice accuracy falls below chance on every individual run, with mean floor accuracy of 27.727.7 percent.

It also does not depend on the particular prompts. For Pythia 160M, using new names and new sentence templates gives a floor accuracy of 34.234.2 percent. Using the new templates with the original names gives 30.030.0 percent. Appendix B.4 lists the names and templates used for these evaluations. Finally, we choose the floor checkpoint using one set of names and evaluate it using a separate set of names. This selects the same checkpoint, showing that the observed minimum is not an artefact of choosing and testing the checkpoint on the same examples.

These checks show that the below-chance window is a repeatable feature of the training trajectory rather than a peculiarity of one run or one evaluation set. Further controls in Appendix B show that the causal reversal at the second mention survives hand-written varied-syntax prompts, and that the behavioural window persists when candidate names span multiple tokens and are scored by full-name log probability.

3.3 The causal role of the second subject mention reverses over training

Having established the behavioural window, we next ask where in the prompt the relevant internal representation has a causal role that changes across training. We intervene separately at the first subject mention S​1S1, the second subject mention S​2S2, the indirect object I​OIO, and a structural control position given by the token immediately after S​1S1.

For the main S​2S2 intervention, we use residual-stream activation patching. We call the evaluated prompt the destination and the prompt supplying the replacement activation the source. For example, the destination may contain “Mary and John … John gave a drink to,” while the source contains “Mary and John … Alice gave a drink to.” The source preserves the sentence structure and the once-mentioned name while replacing the second occurrence of the repeated name. It is used only to supply the activation at S​2S2. Its own next-token prediction is not evaluated, and no correctness label for the source prompt is used. For each layer ℓ\ell in a fixed layer band BB, we replace the destination residual-stream activation at S​2S2 with the corresponding source activation,

hℓ,S​2dest←hℓ,S​2source.h_{\ell,S2}^{\mathrm{dest}}\leftarrow h_{\ell,S2}^{\mathrm{source}}.

The destination tokens and scoring remain unchanged, and the remainder of the forward pass proceeds normally.

We use layers 3 to 5 at 160M, 6 to 10 at 410M, and 4 to 8 at 1B, keeping each band fixed across checkpoints rather than selecting it separately at the floor and maturity. In a separate sensitivity analysis, we repeat the intervention across four non-overlapping layer bands in the separately trained 160M model at step 2000. The effect is positive in every band, although it is smaller in the final band. This shows that the positive early effect in this model is not restricted to the main layer band, while its magnitude still varies with depth. Appendix C.2 reports this analysis, while Appendix C gives the bands used at larger scales.

We also perform a second S​2S2 intervention that does not use a source prompt. At each patched layer, we replace the destination activation with an independently sampled Gaussian vector that is rescaled to match the norm of the clean activation for that prompt, layer, and position. This disrupts the S​2S2 activation without importing information from another prompt.

At the 160M floor, the unmodified model has a mean logit difference of −0.753-0.753, indicating an average preference for the repeated name. Matched S​2S2 activation patching raises the mean to +0.200+0.200, a change of +0.953+0.953. The intervention therefore reverses the direction of the model’s average preference. Random S​2S2 replacement produces almost the same result, raising the mean logit difference to +0.167+0.167, a change of +0.920+0.920.

The pattern reverses at maturity. The unmodified mature model has a mean logit difference of +3.790+3.790, indicating a strong average preference for the correct name. Matched and random S​2S2 replacement reduce this value to −0.333-0.333 and −0.336-0.336, corresponding to changes of −4.123-4.123 and −4.126-4.126. Thus, disrupting the S​2S2 state improves the relative preference at the floor but harms it after training. The close agreement between the matched and random replacements indicates that the reversal is driven by disrupting the S​2S2 state rather than by transferring a particular alternative name from the source prompt.

We next apply the same random replacement at the other positions. At S​1S1, the effect remains positive, changing from +2.152+2.152 at the floor to +2.079+2.079 at maturity. At I​OIO, it remains negative, changing from −3.536-3.536 to −9.063-9.063. At the structural control position, it also remains negative, changing from −0.815-0.815 to −4.450-4.450. These positions can have large causal effects, but none changes sign between the floor and maturity (Figure 2).

This experiment localises the reversal to the causal role of the S​2S2 activation. Because activation patching replaces the entire residual representation at S​2S2, it cannot tell us whether the harmful information reflects repetition, lexical identity, a particular attention-head contribution, or another feature. Section 4 next asks which component causes the repeated-name preference at the floor.

4 Writing the Repeated Name Is Causally Harmful

4.1 Testing the harmful contribution without a donor name

We first test whether, at the floor, a fixed set of attention heads makes a prompt-specific contribution that causally increases the model’s preference for the repeated name. Section 4.3 then tests whether this harmful contribution specifically tracks the identity of the repeated subject supplied at its earlier mention.

We identify candidate heads using prompts that are separate from the later causal evaluation. On a selection split, we replace every attention head individually and retain heads whose replacement improves both the correct name’s probability and the three-name margin, defined as the correct-name logit minus the larger of the repeated-name and unrelated-name logits. This leaves 21 of 144 heads in the official 160M model, 12 of 144 in the separately trained 160M model, 17 of 384 at 410M, and 22 of 128 at 1B. We then rank the surviving heads by their replacement effect on a separate validation split and freeze the resulting set before evaluating any reported effect on held-out prompts. Appendix D.1 gives the full three-stage selection procedure.

This selection identifies heads whose prompt-specific contribution is harmful under the replacement intervention. It does not establish that they copy the repeated name’s identity. We test that stronger claim separately in Section 4.3.

A simple causal test would replace each selected head’s output with the output from another prompt. That design has an important confound. The donor prompt can itself carry a particular name, so an apparent improvement could result from inserting a competing identity rather than removing the harmful prompt-specific contribution of the selected heads.

We therefore use a control-mean replacement. After the head set has been frozen, the remaining names and sentence templates are divided into two disjoint groups. One group is used only to construct the replacement vectors, and the other is used only for evaluation. The two groups share neither names nor templates.

For the control-mean group, we use versions of the prompts in which the two relevant name positions contain different names rather than the same repeated name. Both name orders are included. For each frozen head, we average its output vector at END over all of these prompts, producing one fixed vector per head. Because this vector is averaged across many name pairs and both orders, it is not tied to a particular donor prompt or donor name.

We then evaluate on the separate held-out group, using prompts in which one name is repeated as in the original task. At END, the prompt-specific output of every frozen head is replaced by that head’s fixed control mean, after which the rest of the forward pass proceeds normally. The intervention therefore asks whether removing the selected heads’ prompt-specific contribution improves the model’s preference without inserting a particular competing identity. Appendix D sets out this separation in full.

We measure the effect in two ways. The first is the change in the two-name logit difference LD\mathrm{LD} defined in Section 2. The second is a stricter three-name margin. Let A​L​TALT be a third name that does not appear in the prompt. We define

margin3=ℓ⁡(I​O)−max⁡{ℓ⁡(S),ℓ⁡(A​L​T)},\mathrm{margin}_{3}=\ell(IO)-\max\{\ell(S),\,\ell(ALT)\}, (2)

where ℓ⁡(⋅)\ell(\cdot) is the final-token logit. An increase in LD\mathrm{LD} can occur simply because the repeated name falls, even if another unrelated name becomes more competitive. The three-name margin guards against this by requiring the correct name to improve relative to both the repeated name and the unrelated alternative.

We report 95 percent intervals from template-to-item nested resampling. This procedure resamples sentence templates before resampling items within each selected template, so prompts sharing a template remain grouped. Appendix D gives the complete procedure and the corresponding item-clustered results.

4.2 The replacement improves behaviour at every floor

Replacing the frozen heads’ prompt-specific outputs with their control means improves the I​OIO versus SS logit difference at all four evaluated floors. The changes are +0.180+0.180 for the separately trained 160M model, +0.804+0.804 for official 160M, +0.285+0.285 for 410M, and +0.381+0.381 for 1B, with every template-aware 95 percent interval above zero.

The stricter three-name margin has the same positive direction in all four settings, although its template-aware interval lies above zero only for official 160M and 410M. The uniform conclusion is therefore that the selected heads causally worsen the model’s preference for the correct name relative to the repeated name. Full intervals and both uncertainty analyses are reported in Appendix D.

4.3 Evidence that the selected heads copy name identity

The experiment above establishes that their prompt-specific outputs worsen the correct-versus-repeated preference and that replacing them improves behaviour. It does not by itself show that the heads carry the identity of the name they read. A head could instead correlate with the repeated-name logit for some less specific reason.

We test name-identity transfer with a source-specific intervention. For a target prompt in which the same name appears at both subject positions, we construct a donor prompt that leaves the identity at S​2S2 unchanged but substitutes the other name at S​1S1. We then replace only the frozen heads’ value vectors at S​1S1 with those from the donor. The target prompt, the identity at S​2S2, and all downstream computation are otherwise left unchanged.

If these heads merely happened to raise the repeated-name logit, changing the identity supplied at their source would not require their downstream contribution to follow the substituted name. Instead, the contribution does follow the substituted identity. At every floor, changing the identity supplied at S​1S1 moves the ensemble’s contribution away from the original repeated name and toward the substituted name. The resulting change in the three-name margin is +0.412+0.412 at the retrained 160M model, +0.972+0.972 at official 160M, +0.596+0.596 at 410M, and +0.212+0.212 at 1B. Both the item-clustered and the template-to-item nested intervals lie above zero in all four settings. Appendix D gives both sets of intervals.

The selected heads therefore do more than correlate with a high repeated-name logit. Their contribution follows the identity supplied at the source position, which is why we describe them as copying heads. Appendix F tests several simpler alternative explanations. We next ask what changes during training as the model recovers.

5 Suppression Develops Later

Section 4 showed that repeated-name writing is already harmful at the floor. We now ask what changes as the model recovers. In the mature model, some attention heads help by lowering the repeated name. We therefore identify the head that makes the largest such contribution at maturity and trace that same head backward through training.

5.1 Finding the mature suppressing head

At the mature checkpoint we test each attention head one at a time. We replace the vector produced by that head with its average over the prompts and token positions of each sentence-template block, leaving the rest of the model unchanged, and measure how much this weakens the preference for the correct name over the repeated name. The head whose replacement produces the largest drop is selected as the mature suppressing head.

This procedure selects L8H9 at 160M, L12H12 at 410M, and L11H0 at 1B. We then examine what these heads do in the unmodified mature model. All three behave as expected of a head that helps suppress the repeated name. From the final prediction position END they attend strongly to the second occurrence of the repeated name, with mean attention 0.9340.934 at 160M, 0.3360.336 at 410M, and 0.5270.527 at 1B. Their outputs also point in a direction that lowers the repeated name’s logit, with direct output projections of −6.22-6.22, −2.10-2.10, and −7.27-7.27. These measurements characterise the selected heads rather than confirming the selection, since the replacement effect used to choose them is a causal quantity and the two descriptive quantities are reported alongside it.

5.2 The mature suppressing head is weakly engaged at the floor

We next trace each mature-selected head backward through training without choosing a new head at earlier checkpoints. This lets us ask when the computation that matters at maturity first becomes active.

At the 160M floor the mature suppressing head places only 0.00880.0088 of its attention from END on the second mention and its direct output projection on the repeated name is only −0.034-0.034. One thousand steps later, as behaviour begins to recover, its attention rises to 0.8490.849 and its projection grows to −1.338-1.338. By maturity these reach 0.9340.934 and −6.22-6.22.

The same contrast appears at the other primary sizes. At the 410M floor the head places 0.0620.062 of its attention on the second mention with projection −0.005-0.005, rising to 0.7220.722 and −0.246-0.246 at the next measured checkpoint. At 1B, where the trajectory is sparser, the quantities move from 0.0140.014 and −0.025-0.025 at the floor to 0.5270.527 and −7.27-7.27 at maturity.

The trajectory is therefore not identical across sizes, and the 1B checkpoints do not resolve its detailed shape. What is consistent is the contrast between the floor and later training. The computation that strongly suppresses the repeated name at maturity is barely engaged when the model is most wrong, and becomes substantial around recovery.

5.3 The suppressing head contributes substantially at maturity

Using the same replacement procedure, replacing the selected head lowers the mature logit difference by 2.662.66 at 160M, 1.761.76 at 410M, and 1.591.59 at 1B. The model does not lose the behaviour entirely: forced-choice accuracy remains 0.780.78, 0.900.90, and 0.990.99. The head therefore contributes substantially to the strength of the mature preference without being solely responsible for mature behaviour.

Replacing the selected head substantially weakens the mature preference while forced-choice accuracy remains above chance at all three sizes. The head is therefore an important part of the recovered computation, while other components also contribute.

5.4 Mature suppressor parameters partially rescue the floor

The results above show that the suppressing computation is weak at the floor and strong later, but not whether the changes this head learns are themselves enough to improve the early model.

We therefore take the parameters learned by the mature suppressing head and place them into the same head at the floor checkpoint, replacing its query, key, value, and output parameters with their mature values. Everything else in the floor model is unchanged, and the early model then runs normally using its own activations. The intervention changes what the head has learned rather than inserting an activation produced by the mature model.

The result is a substantial partial rescue at all three sizes. At 160M the logit difference moves from −0.753-0.753 at the floor to +0.849+0.849. At 410M it moves from −0.702-0.702 to +1.876+1.876, and at 1B from −0.543-0.543 to +0.984+0.984. These changes close 35.335.3, 67.967.9, and 40.540.5 percent of the distance between the floor and mature logit differences, and forced-choice accuracy rises to 0.6870.687, 0.8930.893, and 0.8100.810.

The rescue is large but incomplete. The mature suppressing head contains learned changes sufficient to reverse the early preference on many prompts, yet the recovered model cannot be reduced to this head alone. Appendix H gives additional controls, including a matched activation experiment and parameter transplants into unrelated heads.

At the floor, repeated-name writing is already causally harmful while the computation that later suppresses that name is almost absent. During recovery suppression becomes strongly engaged, and giving the early model the mature suppressor parameters moves its behaviour substantially toward the mature state. The below-chance window is therefore best understood as a temporary imbalance between two computations that develop at different times, rather than as the mature circuit operating more weakly.

6 Scope Beyond the Primary Models

The detailed copying and suppression account above is established for Pythia 160M, 410M, and 1B. We next ask whether the same broad developmental pattern appears at other scales, in other model families, and on other tasks. These experiments test the pattern rather than whether every setting contains the same heads.

6.1 Across scale and model family

Early sensitivity to repetition extends across Pythia scale, though not every size is tested under the same intervention. Using first-feed-forward-block replacement, that is the layer-0 MLP, we replace its output at 70M, 160M, 410M, 1B, and 1.4B with the corresponding output from a matched prompt in which the name is not repeated. This improves the floor logit difference at every size, with all five intervals above zero, while the unmodified floor logit difference is negative in every case. At 2.8B, replacing the second occurrence of the repeated name with a different name in the input improves the floor logit difference by +0.456+0.456, while the same edit changes it by −4.076-4.076 at maturity. Matched second-mention state replacement reverses in the same way at 6.9B and 12B, changing the logit difference by +0.837+0.837 and +0.434+0.434 at their floors and by −4.118-4.118 and −3.955-3.955 at maturity. Resampling the outputs of the early feed-forward blocks separately raises floor accuracy from 0.2970.297 to 0.6030.603. Repetition-sensitive information is therefore harmful early across a wider range of Pythia sizes. At 2.8B the input-edit effect additionally reverses by maturity.

The same ordering appears in two independently trained GPT-2 models released by the Stanford CRFM Mistral project (Karamcheti et al., 2021). At step 1500, replacing the first feed-forward block output with its non-repeated counterpart improves the logit difference by +1.123+1.123 and +1.472+1.472 in the two runs. At the same point, replacing the head that later becomes the mature suppressor changes the logit difference by approximately zero. At maturity the first intervention instead changes the logit difference by −4.081-4.081 and −4.607-4.607, while replacing the mature suppressing heads changes it by −1.928-1.928 and −1.506-1.506. The suppressing head differs between the runs, as do the detailed recovery trajectories. What repeats is the order in which the two computations become important.

OLMo-1B (Groeneveld et al., 2024) provides a third family. At its early checkpoint, forced-choice accuracy is 0.4370.437 and the logit difference is −0.220-0.220. Replacing the residual-stream activation at the second occurrence of the repeated name with the corresponding activation from a matched non-repeated prompt improves the logit difference by +0.0448+0.0448, with interval [+0.0349,+0.0549][+0.0349,+0.0549]. At maturity the same intervention changes it by −5.137-5.137, with interval [−5.257,−5.018][-5.257,-5.018]. The causal role of that activation therefore also reverses over training outside the Pythia and GPT-2 families. Appendix J gives the full protocol for each setting.

6.2 Across tasks

A related reversal appears on Greater-Than (Hanna et al., 2023). For a prompt such as “The war lasted from the year 1723 to the year 17”, the model should prefer a completion greater than 23. We construct a matched prompt with a different starting year and replace the residual-stream activation at the token carrying the starting year’s final two digits with the corresponding activation from that matched prompt. At step 1000 this improves the task score by +0.082+0.082, +0.097+0.097, and +0.319+0.319 at 160M, 410M, and 1B. At maturity the same intervention changes the score by −0.737-0.737, −0.667-0.667, and −0.732-0.732. The 410M model is already above chance at the early checkpoint, with accuracy 0.5530.553, so that setting shows a reversal in what the state contributes rather than another below-chance behavioural window.

Taken together, these results support a recurring developmental pattern rather than a single circuit shared across models and tasks. Information that is harmful, or useful to disrupt, early in training can become useful later, while computations that matter at maturity can be weak during the earlier failure. The detailed account in which repeated-name copying is followed by the later development of suppression remains specific to the three primary Pythia models.

7 Related Work

Mechanistic interpretability increasingly examines how model computations develop during training. Saphra and Lopez (2019) track the emergence of linguistic representations, Olsson et al. (2022) connect the formation of induction heads with in-context learning, and Nanda et al. (2023) identify gradual internal changes underlying grokking. Tigges et al. (2024) further show that broad algorithms and functional roles can remain stable across training and scale even when the individual components implementing them change. Together, these studies show that internal structure can develop gradually and need not be fully understood from the final checkpoint. We extend this developmental view to a temporary failure in which behaviour becomes worse than at both earlier and later checkpoints, and we investigate the causal computations that create and resolve that failure.

Our analysis also builds on prior work on the mature IOI circuit. Wang et al. (2023) identify attention heads that move candidate names toward the output and suppress the repeated subject in GPT-2 Small. McDougall et al. (2024) examine copy suppression more broadly and show how attention heads can reduce support for tokens promoted by earlier components. These studies establish the mature copying and suppression mechanisms that motivate our analysis. We examine how their causal balance changes during training and find that repeated-name writing is already harmful when behaviour reaches its floor, while the suppressing computation that later supports the correct answer is still weak.

Our experiments draw on causal mediation, interchange interventions, activation patching, and path patching (Vig et al., 2020; Geiger et al., 2021; Meng et al., 2022; Conmy et al., 2023; Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023). Prior work has shown that conclusions from these methods can depend on the replacement used and the quantity being measured (Zhang and Nanda, 2024; Heimersheim and Nanda, 2024). We therefore use separate interventions for separate causal questions. Control-mean replacement tests whether selected head outputs are harmful, source-position value replacement tests whether their contribution follows a name’s identity, and parameter transplantation tests whether a computation learned later can improve the earlier model.

8 Discussion

Our results show that the mechanism visible at the end of training can give an incomplete picture of how a behaviour developed. At the floor, repeated-name copying is already harmful while the suppressing computation that matters at maturity is still weak. As training continues that balance changes. Intermediate checkpoints can therefore contain causal structure that is largely invisible from the final model alone.

More broadly, Section 6 shows related early-to-late reversals across additional model sizes, GPT-2, OLMo, and Greater-Than. We do not read this as evidence for one shared circuit across all settings. It suggests a broader developmental pattern in which information or computations that are harmful, or useful to disrupt, early in training can later become useful as other parts of the model develop. For mechanistic interpretability, this makes the timing of a computation’s contribution as important as its role in the final model.

9 Conclusion

During the below-chance window, repeated-name copying is already causally harmful while the suppression that later supports correct behaviour is still weak. As the model recovers, suppression becomes important, and giving the early model the mature suppressor parameters partially moves its behaviour toward the mature state. These results show that the mechanisms governing behaviour during training can differ substantially from those visible at the final checkpoint, motivating mechanistic analysis of how circuits develop rather than only how they operate once training is complete.

Limitations

Our strongest causal account is established for the naming task in the Pythia 160M, 410M, and 1B models. Additional Pythia scales, two independently trained GPT-2 models, OLMo, and Greater-Than show related developmental reversals, but we do not establish that they use the same copying and suppression mechanism. The broader evidence supports a recurring pattern across training rather than a universal circuit shared across models and tasks.

The interventions also answer different causal questions. Replacing the residual-stream state at the second name mention localises where information affecting the prediction is carried, but does not identify a duplication-specific feature. The copying claim instead rests on interventions on a selected set of attention heads, replacing their prompt-specific outputs and changing the identity supplied at the source position. These give stronger evidence for repeated-name copying, but the head-level account is limited to the primary models.

Our analysis explains the below-chance behaviour as an imbalance between harmful copying and weak suppression, but not why training develops copying first. Suppression may become useful only after the model develops a pathway that makes the repeated candidate available, or the order may be driven by the training data. Distinguishing these possibilities would require changing the data or intervening during training to change how copying develops, then measuring the effect on suppression.

Finally, our experiments focus on relatively small open-weight models and structured tasks. For the released Pythia runs, checkpoints around the behavioural transition are spaced 1000 steps apart, limiting how precisely we can localise when computations emerge or change causal role. This leaves open how often the same pattern appears in larger models, less structured behaviour, or settings with sparser checkpoints.

Appendix A Protocols and Manipulations

A.1 Prompt construction

We follow the prompt construction of Wang et al. (2023). Each prompt instantiates a sentence template with two distinct first names that each correspond to a single token. One name appears twice, at S​1S1 and S​2S2, while the other appears once and is the correct continuation at END. Figure 5 gives a concrete example.

For each template and name pair, we balance which name is repeated and which is the correct once-mentioned name. This prevents either the identity or the earlier position of a name from determining the answer. When an experiment requires separate prompts for selection, replacement construction, and final evaluation, the relevant names and sentence templates are partitioned before the intervention is evaluated. The experiment-specific sections give the exact split used in each case.

A.2 Models and checkpoints

Our primary mechanistic analyses use the released Pythia 160M, 410M, and 1B models (Biderman et al., 2023). We additionally use a separately trained 160M model with the same architecture and tokenizer but more frequent checkpoints around the early transition. This model helps resolve when the relevant computations change, but the main phenomenon and the cross-scale conclusions do not depend on that run.

Additional Pythia sizes from 70M through 12B are used for the scale analyses described in the corresponding appendices. Appendix J separately gives the model and checkpoint details for the GPT-2 and OLMo experiments.

For each run, the floor is the evaluated checkpoint with the lowest forced-choice accuracy. It occurs at step 2000 for the released 160M and 410M models, step 1000 for 1B, and step 2850 for the separately trained 160M model. We call the final checkpoint the mature checkpoint, and the first evaluated checkpoint after the floor at which forced-choice accuracy exceeds 50%50\% the recovery checkpoint.

A.3 Intervention glossary

The experiments below modify different parts of the model and answer different causal questions. We therefore use a distinct name for each intervention and specify both the quantity being replaced and the source of its replacement.

Input token edit.

The token sequence itself is changed before the model runs. For example, the second occurrence of the repeated name can be replaced by a third name. This tests sensitivity to the repetition in the input, but does not identify where or how the model uses that information. Figure 13 shows the edit on the canonical prompt, with the token that changes marked.

Residual-stream state replacement.

The residual-stream activation at one token position is replaced across a specified band of layers. The replacement can come from a matched prompt or from an independently sampled direction whose magnitude is matched to the original activation. This localises where a causally important state is carried, but changing the entire state does not identify which feature within it matters.

First feed-forward block activation replacement.

The output of the first block’s feed-forward module is replaced with the corresponding output from a matched prompt in which the name is not repeated. The evaluated prompt itself is unchanged. This tests whether repetition-sensitive information computed early in the network is harmful, without treating the intervention as an input edit.

Control-mean head-output replacement.

For the copying experiment in Section 4, each frozen head’s output at END is replaced with one fixed vector computed by averaging that head’s output over separate non-repeated control prompts. Because the average spans many names and both name orders, it is not tied to any particular donor identity. This tests whether the selected heads’ prompt-specific contribution is causally harmful.

Source-position value replacement.

To test whether that contribution actually follows the copied name, we replace only the frozen heads’ value vectors at S​1S1 with those from a prompt carrying a different name there. The target prompt, the identity at S​2S2, and downstream computation remain unchanged. If the downstream contribution follows the substituted identity, the intervention provides direct evidence of name copying.

Passive attention split.

The total attention assigned to S​1S1 and S​2S2 is preserved but divided equally between the two positions, while their value vectors remain unchanged. This tests whether the observed attenuation requires a learned routing decision beyond the mechanical distribution of a fixed amount of attention across two positions.

Mature-head mean replacement.

In the mature-suppressor experiments, the selected head’s activation is replaced by its mean over the prompts and token positions of each sentence-template block. This differs from the separate control-prompt mean used in the copying experiment above. It measures how strongly the mature model depends on the selected head.

Activation graft.

An activation at a chosen site is replaced by the corresponding activation produced by another checkpoint of the same model on the same prompts. This asks whether the later activation itself is sufficient to change earlier behaviour.

Parameter transplant.

The query, key, value, and output parameters of one attention head are replaced with those of the same head at another checkpoint. The receiving model then computes its own activations normally. Our main use copies the mature suppressor’s parameters into the floor model and asks whether what the head learned later is sufficient to improve early behaviour.

Route isolation.

A specific route between two components is isolated while alternative routes are held fixed by the intervention. This estimates how much of a measured dependence travels through that particular route.

A.4 Uncertainty and resampling

We use several resampling procedures depending on the structure of the evaluation set. A prompt bootstrap resamples individual prompts. An item-clustered bootstrap instead keeps paired evaluations of the same item together before resampling, so closely related observations are not treated as independent.

For the copying experiments, prompts also share sentence templates. We therefore report a stricter template-to-item nested bootstrap that first resamples templates and then resamples items within each selected template. The intervals quoted in the main text use this procedure with ten thousand bootstrap draws.

Because the released settings contain only three template groups and the separately trained setting contains four, these nested intervals rest on a small number of top-level groups. We therefore report the item-clustered intervals alongside them rather than treating either procedure as the sole uncertainty estimate.

Appendix B Behavioural Characterisation and Robustness

This appendix gives additional evidence that the below-chance window is a genuine and repeatable change in the model’s preference between the two task-relevant names. We examine the full output distribution, ordinary language-model loss, independently varied training runs, and evaluations using prompts separated from those used elsewhere in the analysis.

B.1 Full-vocabulary behaviour at the floor

Forced-choice accuracy compares only the correct name I​OIO and the repeated name SS. We therefore examine the complete next-token distribution to determine what the below-chance result means outside that two-name comparison.

At the 160M floor, the repeated name receives mean probability 0.02380.0238, compared with 0.01180.0118 for the correct name. Its mean vocabulary rank is also better, 14.914.9 compared with 29.429.4 for the correct name. Greedy decoding, however, produces neither candidate on 98.6798.67 percent of prompts. Figure 8 shows the probability comparison at the floor.

The below-chance window therefore describes a reversal in the relative preference between the two task-relevant names. At the floor, the repeated name is preferred to the correct name even though neither candidate is usually selected by greedy decoding. Figure 9 follows the candidates’ vocabulary ranks across training. The repeated name is ranked ahead around the floor, after which the correct name overtakes it during recovery.

Logit difference is also not an artefact of using unnormalised logits. Because the correct and repeated names are scored at the same next-token position in the same forward pass, the normalising constant of the softmax is shared between them, so log⁡p⁡(I​O)−log⁡p⁡(S)=zI​O−zS=LD\log p(IO)-\log p(S)=z_{IO}-z_{S}=\mathrm{LD} exactly. We compute the two quantities independently and verify this equality numerically at every evaluated checkpoint. As a separate scale-free check, the repeated name also outranks the correct name in the full vocabulary at each primary-model floor. Using rank 1 for the highest-scoring token, the median repeated-name and correct-name ranks are 7 against 13 at 160M, 10 against 24.5 at 410M, and 57 against 98 at 1B, with floor accuracies of 0.3170.317, 0.2930.293, and 0.3630.363. The below-chance ordering therefore appears in the normalised log-probability ratio and in vocabulary rank alike, rather than depending on the numerical scale of the logits.

B.2 Language-model loss continues to improve

We next ask whether the failure on this task coincides with a broader deterioration in next-token prediction. We evaluate the released Pythia 160M checkpoints on a fixed sample of Pile text drawn from the same corpus that Pythia was pretrained on.

Mean language-model loss decreases from 3.7343.734 at step 1000 to 3.1403.140, 2.9642.964, 2.8012.801, and 2.6772.677 at steps 2000, 3000, 5000, and 10000. The decrease is monotonic across the checkpoints spanning the floor and recovery.

The below-chance window therefore occurs while language-model loss on a fixed text sample continues to improve. This does not imply that every other capability improves over the same interval, but it rules out worsening language-model loss on this sample as an explanation for the reversal. The IOI reversal therefore occurs while aggregate next-token loss on the sampled Pile text continues to improve. Appendix K compares the trajectories of other structured tasks over the same training period.

B.3 Robustness across training runs

The window also persists across independently varied training runs. We evaluate nine PolyPythia 160M variants (van der Wal et al., 2025). Three change the random seed, three change the order of the training data, and three change the parameter initialisation. Across all nine runs, mean accuracy at the floor is 27.727.7 percent.

We additionally apply the input token edit defined in Appendix A.3, replacing the second occurrence of the repeated name with a different name. This improves the floor logit difference in all nine runs, with mean change +1.076+1.076 and standard deviation 0.2670.267. Figure 10 shows the effects grouped by the aspect of training that was varied.

The below-chance preference and its sensitivity to the repeated relation therefore survive changes in the random seed, data order, and parameter initialisation. This experiment establishes behavioural and input-level robustness across the nine runs. The head-level copying mechanism is evaluated separately in Appendix D. Table 1 reports the individual results for all nine runs.

B.4 Robustness to new names and templates

We test this robustness on Pythia 160M. With both new names and new templates, floor accuracy is 34.234.2 percent. Using the new templates with the original names gives 30.030.0 percent. In both cases accuracy later recovers to near ceiling.

Evaluation material.

We use four new sentence templates that do not appear in the primary evaluation:

  1. 1.

    “After the meeting, {S} and {IO} grabbed coffee, and {S} handed the cup to”

  2. 2.

    “At the party, {IO} and {S} were chatting, and {S} passed a drink to”

  3. 3.

    “During the trip, {S} and {IO} shared a cab, and {S} gave directions to”

  4. 4.

    “In the lab, {IO} and {S} ran the test, and {S} showed the result to”

For the new-template and new-name evaluation, the names are Daniel, Rachel, Kevin, Laura, Brian, Nicole, Steven, Megan, Jason, Emily, Aaron, and Diana. For the new-template-only evaluation, the names are John, Mary, Tom, Anna, Paul, and Lucy. We retain only names that correspond to a single token under the Pythia tokenizer.

There is a separate concern when defining the floor itself. Because the floor is chosen as the checkpoint with the lowest accuracy on this task, selecting and evaluating it on the same prompts could exaggerate the depth of the minimum. We therefore select the floor using one set of names and evaluate the resulting checkpoint on a separate name set. The independently selected floor is the same checkpoint.

These controls show that the observed window is not tied to the particular names or sentence templates in the primary evaluation, and is not an artefact of selecting the minimum on the same examples used to report it.

B.5 Robustness to naturalised wording

The preceding controls change the names and templates within the benchmark family. We additionally test whether the phenomenon survives substantially less stereotyped wording, using hand-written sentences with varied syntax. Each prompt still contains one candidate name once and the competing subject twice, but the surrounding phrasing is written independently rather than instantiated from the primary template set. We require both names to be single tokens, verify the repeated-name structure after tokenisation, and locate the second mention directly in each sequence rather than assuming a fixed offset. Thirty-four prompts pass these checks. We evaluate the three primary Pythia sizes at their respective floors and at maturity, applying the same matched residual-state intervention at the second mention and the same model-specific layer bands used in the main analysis.

The reversal survives this change in wording. Floor accuracy is 0.0290.029, 0.1470.147, and 0.1470.147 at 160M, 410M, and 1B respectively, so the behaviour is below chance on these prompts at every size. At 160M the intervention improves the logit difference by +0.882+0.882 with interval [0.626,1.164][0.626,1.164], while at maturity the effect reverses to −2.150-2.150 with [−2.912,−1.391][-2.912,-1.391]. The corresponding floor-to-mature effects are +0.344+0.344 [0.165,0.545][0.165,0.545] to −3.899-3.899 [−4.330,−3.475][-4.330,-3.475] at 410M, and +0.403+0.403 [0.292,0.528][0.292,0.528] to −1.565-1.565 [−2.254,−0.911][-2.254,-0.911] at 1B. Every floor interval is strictly positive and every mature interval strictly negative, so the below-chance behaviour and the causal reversal at the second mention are not restricted to the rigid sentence templates of the primary benchmark. These hand-written prompts establish robustness to substantially varied syntax, while broader natural-text generalisation remains a separate question.

B.6 Robustness to multi-token names

The primary experiments restrict the candidate names to single tokens so that the two candidates can be compared at one next-token position. To test whether the behavioural dip depends on that restriction, we construct prompts whose candidate names each contain exactly two tokens. Candidate first-name and surname combinations are filtered through the model tokenizer, leaving 178 valid two-token names, and 120 prompts are sampled across three sentence frames. Rather than scoring only the first token, we teacher-force each complete candidate continuation and sum the log probabilities of its two tokens. The resulting score is the full-name log-probability margin between the correct and repeated names.

Under this score the model remains strongly below chance at the 160M floor. At step 2000 the mean margin is −2.255-2.255 with interval [−2.553,−1.954][-2.553,-1.954], and only 7.57.5 percent of prompts favour the correct complete name. At step 3000 the margin remains negative at −1.192-1.192 with [−1.550,−0.832][-1.550,-0.832] and accuracy 26.726.7 percent, before recovering by maturity to +2.848+2.848 with [2.507,3.197][2.507,3.197] and accuracy 93.393.3 percent. The temporary preference reversal therefore survives when candidate answers span multiple tokens and are scored as complete names. This experiment is behavioural only. Extending the causal intervention at the second mention to multi-token continuations would require a separate intervention and scoring protocol, and we do not claim that the causal reversal has been tested here.

Together with the held-out-name, held-out-template, and naturalised-prompt controls above, these results rule out rigid template wording and single-token answer scoring as explanations for the behavioural window, while keeping the stronger copying-to-suppression claims scoped to the interventions tested in the main analysis.

Appendix C The Second-Mention State and Input Controls

C.1 Position controls

The replaced activations are the residual-stream outputs of an early band of transformer blocks. The band covers layers 3 to 5 of 12 at 160M, layers 6 to 10 of 24 at 410M, layers 4 to 8 of 16 at 1B, and layers 8 to 14 at 2.8B and 6.9B, and layers 9 to 16 at 12B. At 6.9B and 12B, forced-choice accuracy falls below chance at step 2000, to 0.3230.323 and 0.4200.420. Matched second-mention state replacement changes the logit difference by +0.837+0.837 and +0.434+0.434 at those floors, and by −4.118-4.118 and −3.955-3.955 at step 143000. A separate replacement vector is drawn for every prompt and every layer in the band. Figure 11 sets the two variants side by side on the canonical prompt. Figure 12 marks the four tested sites on one sentence.

Table 2 reports the controls. Replacement at the second subject mention improves the logit difference by 0.9530.953 at the floor and harms it by 4.1234.123 at maturity. Replacing the same activations with a Gaussian vector rescaled to the magnitude of what it replaces, drawn independently per prompt, gives 0.9200.920 and −4.126-4.126. The two agree to within a few hundredths at both checkpoints.

That agreement determines what the experiment establishes. The random direction is sampled independently while its norm is taken from the state it replaces, so it imports no content from another prompt. Its reproducing the matched effect therefore shows the result depends on disrupting the activation rather than on supplying different name content. The remaining positions show no sign reversal.

C.2 Sensitivity to the layer band

The main 160M intervention uses layers 3 to 5. We test whether the early effect depends strongly on this choice using the separately trained 160M model at step 2000. This checkpoint precedes that model’s floor at step 2850, so we use this experiment only as a sensitivity check on the layer choice rather than as a separate test of the floor-to-mature reversal.

We divide the model’s 12 layers into four non-overlapping three-layer bands and repeat the same matched S​2S2 activation-patching intervention in each band. The change in logit difference is +0.447+0.447 for layers 0–2, +0.388+0.388 for layers 3–5, +0.443+0.443 for layers 6–8, and +0.133+0.133 for layers 9–11. The corresponding 95%95\% intervals are [0.378,0.520][0.378,0.520], [0.322,0.458][0.322,0.458], [0.395,0.496][0.395,0.496], and [0.113,0.153][0.113,0.153]. Each band is evaluated on 300 prompts.

The intervention has a positive effect across all four parts of the network rather than only in the layer band used for the main analysis, although the effect is weaker in the final three layers. This sweep uses its own evaluation set of ten templates with thirty prompts each, so its baseline logit difference differs from that of the main analysis.

C.3 Removing the repetition at the input

A complementary experiment changes the tokens. For each prompt the second occurrence of the subject is replaced by a third single-token name differing from both the subject and the indirect object, which preserves sequence length and every token position while removing the repeated-name relation. On a fixed evaluation set of 800 prompts at the 160M floor this improves the logit difference by 0.8330.833, with a crossed template and name-pair interval of [0.681,1.023][0.681,1.023], and moves forced-choice accuracy from 0.3090.309 to 0.5040.504. The change is driven mainly by lowering the repeated subject, since the subject logit falls by 0.6810.681 while the object logit rises by 0.1520.152, as Figure 14 shows. Because the edit changes repetition status and token identity together, it gives repetition-sensitive evidence without isolating repetition from lexical identity. A control substituting a different third name gives a very similar improvement, and a control editing a nearby filler token gives a much smaller effect.

Appendix D Copying-Head Interventions and Controls

This appendix gives the full protocol behind the copying results in Section 4. We first explain how the head set is selected and how the data used for selection, replacement construction, and evaluation are kept separate. We then give the complete control-mean intervention, the uncertainty analyses, the source-identity experiment, independent functional checks on the heads, and a final comparison that measures copying and suppression using the same intervention.

D.1 Head selection and data separation

Selection proceeds in three stages on disjoint prompts. We first screen candidates by replacing each head individually on a selection set. A head qualifies only if replacing it improves both the three-name margin and the correct name’s probability. We use only the sign of each change at this stage rather than its magnitude, and we do not rank heads by how strongly they write to the output logits. This makes the initial screen intervention-based rather than attribution-based and avoids choosing a magnitude threshold. We then rank the surviving heads by their replacement effect on a separate validation split that took no part in that screen. The resulting set is frozen before any reported effect is measured, and no later experiment changes which heads are intervened on. Figure 16 summarises the four stages and the prompt sets each one uses.

After the head set has been fixed, the remaining names and sentence templates are divided again into two non-overlapping groups. The control-mean group is used only to construct the replacement activation for each selected head. The evaluation group is used only to measure the resulting causal effect. No names or sentence templates are shared between these two groups.

The control-mean prompts are non-repeated variants in which the two relevant name positions contain different names. Both name orders are included so that the resulting average is not tied to one name occupying one fixed role. The held-out evaluation prompts contain the ordinary repeated-name structure.

The protocol therefore separates three roles. One set of prompts is used to select and freeze the head ensemble; a separate set of non-repeated prompts is used to construct the fixed replacement vectors; and held-out repeated-name prompts are used only to measure the final causal effect. Figure 15 summarises this separation. Keeping the names and sentence templates disjoint prevents either head selection or replacement construction from benefiting from the examples on which the effect is finally measured.

This separation matters because the causal test should not benefit from selecting heads, constructing their replacement, and evaluating them on the same names or sentence templates.

D.2 Control-mean replacement

For each frozen attention head we compute one fixed replacement vector by averaging that head’s output at END over the non-repeated prompts in the control-mean group. The average spans multiple names, sentence templates, and both name orders, so it does not correspond to the activation produced by any particular donor prompt or alternative answer.

On each held-out repeated-name prompt we replace the selected heads’ prompt-specific outputs at END with these fixed control means. The rest of the model then proceeds normally.

The intervention is deliberately different from replacing an activation with one taken from another prompt of the same task. A single donor prompt can carry the identity of a particular alternative name and thereby improve the prediction simply by introducing that name. Averaging across many non-repeated controls avoids assigning the replacement to one specific donor identity. We do not need the stronger assumption that every possible name-specific feature cancels exactly in the average. The relevant property is narrower: the replacement is not the activation from a particular prompt carrying a particular competing name. Figure 17 follows one head from the control prompts to its fixed mean and then to the evaluation prompt.

We evaluate the intervention with two outcome measures. The first is the change in the I​OIO versus SS logit difference, Δ​LD=LDreplaced−LDnative\Delta\mathrm{LD}=\mathrm{LD}_{\text{replaced}}-\mathrm{LD}_{\text{native}}, where a positive value means that replacing the heads’ native outputs improves the model’s preference for the correct name relative to the repeated name. The second is the three-name margin of equation 2, where A​L​TALT is an unrelated third name. The stricter measure tests whether an apparent improvement over SS remains when another plausible named competitor is included.

This control-mean replacement should not be confused with the mature-head mean replacement used in Section 5. Here the mean is constructed from a separate set of non-repeated control prompts. There, the selected mature suppressor’s activation is replaced by its mean over the prompts and token positions of each sentence-template block. They are different interventions answering different causal questions. Figure 27 places this mean beside the copying control mean, which is built from different data.

D.3 Replacing the selected heads improves the floor prediction

Control-mean replacement improves the I​OIO versus SS logit difference at all four evaluated floors. The effects are +0.180+0.180 for the separately trained 160M model, +0.804+0.804 for released 160M, +0.285+0.285 for 410M, and +0.381+0.381 for 1B. Under template-to-item nested resampling all four intervals remain above zero. Table 4 gives both measures with their intervals.

The stricter three-name margin has a positive point estimate in all four settings. Its template-aware interval lies above zero for released 160M and 410M, and crosses zero for the separately trained 160M model and for 1B. The uniform conclusion is therefore the two-name result: replacing the selected heads’ prompt-specific outputs improves the model’s preference for the correct name relative to the repeated name.

We additionally report item-clustered intervals, which treat paired contrast rows from the same item as one resampling unit. These are generally narrower than the template-to-item intervals because the latter additionally account for the small number of shared sentence-template groups. Both analyses and their precise resampling definitions are given in Appendix A. Figure 19 compares the two procedures, and Table 7 gives every cell.

These interventions identify a causally harmful contribution from the selected ensemble at the floor. Appendix D.5 next tests whether that contribution follows the identity supplied at the heads’ source position.

Effect later in training.

We apply the same frozen head set and the same replacement procedure at later checkpoints. At recovery and at maturity the strong positive effect seen at the floor becomes much smaller and is no longer consistently positive. The harmful contribution is therefore not a fixed property of these heads throughout training. The importance of a head depends on the surrounding computation in which it participates, which is one reason a head’s role at a single checkpoint should not automatically be treated as its role throughout training.

D.4 Difference between the two-name and three-name measures

The two measures answer related but different questions. The two-name measure asks whether replacing the selected heads improves the correct name relative specifically to the repeated name. The three-name margin additionally requires the correct name to improve relative to an unrelated third candidate. An intervention can therefore strongly improve I​OIO minus SS while producing a smaller change in the three-name margin, if some of the changed logit mass is redistributed toward the third name.

For this reason the two quantities should not be read as interchangeable estimates of one underlying effect. The two-name result is the direct test of the repeated-name preference. The three-name result is a stricter robustness check against an improvement that is specific only to that comparison.

The same distinction matters when comparing this experiment with the source-identity intervention below. The two experiments use the same outcome metric while changing different parts of the model, and therefore estimate different causal effects. Their magnitudes should not be compared as though one were a stronger version of the other.

D.5 The contribution follows the identity supplied at the first mention

The control-mean experiment shows that replacing the selected heads’ outputs improves behaviour, but it does not by itself establish what information those outputs carry. We therefore perform a more targeted intervention that asks whether the heads’ downstream contribution follows the identity of the name they read.

For every target prompt we construct a donor prompt with the same name at S​2S2 but a different name at S​1S1. The two contrasts can be written schematically as X​X←Y​XXX\leftarrow YX and Y​Y←X​YYY\leftarrow XY. The repeated identity at S​2S2 is therefore held fixed while the identity available at the earlier source position changes.

We then replace only the selected heads’ value vectors at S​1S1 with the corresponding value vectors from the donor prompt. The target prompt itself remains unchanged, its S​2S2 token remains unchanged, the rest of the model remains native, and downstream computation proceeds from the modified values.

This asks a more specific question than the control-mean replacement. If the heads merely correlate with a high repeated-name logit, changing the identity supplied at S​1S1 need not make their downstream contribution follow the substituted name. If they carry name identity from S​1S1, however, substituting the value there should redirect which name they support. Figure 20 makes the intervention concrete by placing the target and source prompts side by side and marking the single value vector that is transferred.

Instead, the contribution follows the substituted identity. At every evaluated floor the original repeated name’s logit falls while the substituted name’s logit rises, in the expected opposing directions, and the three-name margin improves. Table 5 gives the component logit changes and Table 6 the three-name margin under both uncertainty procedures.

The uncertainty calculation first averages the two same-S​2S2 contrast rows belonging to each item and then resamples those item-level values. The template-aware analysis additionally resamples the sentence-template groups before resampling items within them.

The key result is not simply that replacing these heads helps. Their downstream contribution changes identity when the identity supplied at their source position changes. This is the evidence that licenses describing the ensemble as performing repeated-name copying rather than merely correlating with the repeated-name logit.

D.6 Independent functional evidence from subject-writing heads

The source-identity intervention above is the direct causal evidence for copying. We also perform a separate functional analysis that does not use that intervention to choose the heads.

At each model size we identify the attention heads that most strongly write the prediction toward the repeated subject at the floor, ranked by their signed direct contribution to the I​OIO minus SS logit difference. We then inspect two properties expected of a copying head: whether the head attends from END to positions containing the repeated subject, and whether its value-output transformation maps the attended subject representation toward that subject’s output direction. These are descriptive diagnostics applied after the subject-writing heads have been identified.

For released Pythia 160M the five leading subject writers are L5H9, L10H7, L5H5, L4H6, and L9H7. Four of the five satisfy the resulting copy-like diagnostic. L5H9, for example, has a subject-copying output score of 0.6740.674 and places substantial attention on the repeated-name positions. At 410M all five leading subject writers satisfy the criterion, and at 1B all five do as well.

These diagnostics provide corroborating evidence. A head can have an output direction that decodes as copying without that decoded direction being the causal quantity responsible for behaviour. Appendix F shows that directly removing a linearly decoded duplication direction makes floor behaviour worse rather than better. The causal copying claim therefore rests on the output replacement and the source-identity intervention, while this analysis provides independent evidence that heads identified because they write toward the repeated subject have the functional properties expected of name-copying heads.

D.7 Copying and suppression measured with the same intervention

The main copying and suppression analyses use different interventions because they answer different causal questions. As an additional comparison we therefore measure frozen copying and suppressing ensembles using the same intervention and the same outcome metric.

Two head sets are used. The first is the frozen floor copying ensemble described above. The second is a separate mature suppressor ensemble, which is not the single mature suppressing head analysed in Section 5. It is obtained from an independent all-head scan at the mature checkpoint in which candidate heads are ranked by the effect of replacing their full output at END using a donor that preserves the S​2S2 identity while changing the earlier name. Candidate suppressors must then reproduce the suppressive sign on a separate validation split, must act by reducing support for the repeated name under the native model, and must have the same sign in both identity-swap directions. The selection and validation criteria are therefore applied before the developmental comparison. This yields 15 validated mature suppressor heads for the separately trained 160M model and 14 for the released 160M model. Neither ensemble is reselected as training proceeds.

For each target prompt the donor keeps the identity at S​2S2 fixed and changes the identity at S​1S1. We then replace the selected ensemble’s full attention-head outputs at END with the outputs produced by that donor, applying the same operation separately to the copying ensemble and to the mature suppressor ensemble. The outcome is the change in the three-name margin. Under this sign convention a positive change means replacement improves behaviour, so the native ensemble was harmful, and a negative change means replacement harms behaviour, so the native ensemble was helping.

In the densely checkpointed separately trained 160M model, the copying ensemble already has a reliably harmful contribution at the earliest evaluated checkpoint. The mature suppressor ensemble becomes reliably helpful only later. The trajectory identifies the first positive-interval copying effect at step 1800 and the first reliably negative suppressor effect at step 6000. These are checkpoint-resolution markers rather than exact circuit birth times.

The released 160M model shows the same qualitative ordering, although the later trajectory of the frozen floor copying set differs. In that model the originally harmful set eventually changes causal sign and becomes useful rather than remaining a fixed harmful pathway. This difference is informative rather than contradictory, since component roles can themselves change during training.

The common result is the developmental ordering. Figure 21 traces both ensembles. A repeated-name-writing contribution is already harmful during the early failure, while the ensemble selected for mature suppression becomes strongly helpful later.

D.8 Evidence for harmful repeated-name copying

The experiments in this appendix progressively narrow the interpretation. Control-mean replacement shows that the selected heads’ prompt-specific outputs causally worsen the floor preference for the correct name relative to the repeated name. The source-identity intervention then shows that their contribution follows the identity supplied at the position from which they read. Independently selected subject-writing heads also predominantly exhibit the attention and output properties expected of copying heads. Finally, measuring frozen copying and suppressing ensembles under a common intervention shows that their causal importance develops at different times.

Together these results support a causally harmful repeated-name copying ensemble at the floor. The selected ensemble need not be unique or complete, and individual heads within it may differ in their precise roles. The later suppression analysis is therefore kept conceptually separate: Section 5 asks how a mature suppressing computation develops and whether giving that computation to the early model can improve its behaviour.

Appendix E Specificity of the Selected Copying Heads

The copying experiment establishes that replacing the selected heads improves behaviour at the floor. A separate question is whether this result is specific to the selected ensemble, or whether almost any set of heads with similar observable properties would produce the same effect.

We test this using feature-matched control sets. For each selected head we construct matched alternatives from other heads in the same layer. Matching uses six quantities measured on a resource-disjoint selection split: the attention from END to the first subject mention, to the second, and to the indirect object; the norm of the head’s output at END; its direct projection toward the repeated name; and the selectivity of its value representation at the first mention for the identity supplied there. We standardise these six features within each layer and rank candidate controls by Euclidean distance from the selected head in that standardised space. The selected heads themselves are excluded. We then construct 200 control ensembles with the same number of heads as the selected ensemble and evaluate every ensemble using the same intervention and the same held-out evaluation prompts.

These controls are more demanding than random-head controls. They ask whether the causal result can be explained simply by choosing heads that attend to names and write strongly at the final position, rather than by the particular heads our selection procedure identifies. The specificity experiment also uses names and sentence templates separated from those used to identify the ensemble.

The selected-set effects here should not be expected to equal those in Appendix D exactly. This experiment uses its own held-out prompts so that the selected set and all 200 matched controls are compared on identical examples. The two appendices therefore estimate the same kind of intervention effect on different evaluation sets.

At the released 160M floor the selected ensemble is clearly separated from the matched controls. Its two-name effect is +1.092+1.092, while the 200 matched control sets range from −0.023-0.023 to +0.056+0.056. On the three-name margin the selected effect is +0.410+0.410, against a control range of −0.023-0.023 to +0.054+0.054. No matched set approaches the selected ensemble on either measure, giving an empirical upper-tail probability of 0.0050.005 for both.

The separation is narrower in the separately trained 160M model. The selected set gives +0.319+0.319 on the two-name measure while the matched controls extend as high as +0.316+0.316, an empirical upper-tail probability of 0.0050.005. On the three-name margin the selected effect is +0.240+0.240 while the controls reach +0.250+0.250, so at least one matched set exceeds the selected ensemble and the empirical upper-tail probability is 0.0150.015, placing the selected set at the 99th percentile rather than beyond every control.

The two settings therefore support different strengths of conclusion. At released 160M the selected ensemble is strongly separated from heads matched on these observable properties. At the separately trained model it is unusual but not cleanly separated from the strongest matched alternatives, particularly on the three-name measure. This agrees with the wider uncertainty seen for that setting in Appendix D. Figure 22 plots the selected set against the control distribution.

These controls show that the selected ensemble is specific relative to the tested feature-matched control family.
