The separation is strong in the released 160M model and narrower in the separately trained model, particularly for the three-name margin. The experiment establishes that the result is not produced by an arbitrary collection of heads with similar observable properties.

Appendix F Alternative Accounts and Boundary Tests

The copying interventions establish that a repeated-name-writing ensemble is causally harmful at the floor. We next test whether several simpler explanations can account for the observations. The first two concern what produces the harmful repeated-name preference. The third asks whether the observed attenuation in attention routing requires an additional learned corrective mechanism.

F.1 Matching-name amplification

One possible explanation is that the model detects that the names at S​1S1 and S​2S2 match and gives the matching identity an additional boost. Such a mechanism predicts superadditivity: putting the same name at both subject positions should promote that name more than the sum of putting it at either position separately.

We test this with a 2×22\times 2 factorial comparison over whether the identity whose logit is measured appears at each of the two subject positions. Let za​bz_{ab} denote that identity’s logit when it is present at the first mention if and only if a=1a=1, and at the second mention if and only if b=1b=1. The interaction is

I=z11−z10−z01+z00,I=z_{11}-z_{10}-z_{01}+z_{00}, (3)

equivalently (z11−z01)−(z10−z00)(z_{11}-z_{01})-(z_{10}-z_{00}), which asks whether placing the identity at both positions gives a boost beyond the sum of the two single-position effects. A positive value is superadditive, zero is additive, and a negative value is subadditive. A positive interaction would be the signature predicted by matching-name amplification. A value near zero would indicate approximately additive contributions, and a negative value indicates that the two occurrences together contribute less than the sum of their separate effects.

The measured interaction is negative at every floor. It is −1.250-1.250 with interval [−1.324,−1.179][-1.324,-1.179] for the separately trained 160M model, −1.052-1.052 with [−1.122,−0.986][-1.122,-0.986] for released 160M, −0.803-0.803 with [−0.860,−0.750][-0.860,-0.750] at 410M, and −0.335-0.335 with [−0.356,−0.313][-0.356,-0.313] at 1B. The tested account therefore predicts the wrong sign, and repetition is subadditive under this measurement rather than superadditive. Figure 24 plots the interaction at each floor.

This does not mean the model contains no information about whether a name has appeared before. It rules out the more specific account tested here, in which matching the two subject identities produces an additional positive boost to the repeated name.

F.2 A linearly decoded duplication direction

A second possibility is that the harmful floor behaviour is carried by a single direction in the residual-stream activation at S​2S2 that linearly encodes whether the name has appeared before.

We fit this direction to repeated and non-repeated second-mention activations from the same 300-prompt 160M floor evaluation used for this control, so it is fitted in distribution rather than held out. The direction is linearly decodable, so information separating repeated from non-repeated cases is present in the activation. Decodability alone, however, does not show that this direction causes the harmful prediction.

We test causality by progressively subtracting the decoded direction from the S​2S2 activation at the 160M floor. If this direction were the harmful quantity responsible for the below-chance preference, removing more of it should improve behaviour.

The opposite occurs. Forced-choice accuracy falls from 0.3170.317 in the unmodified model to 0.2970.297, 0.2900.290, 0.2700.270, and 0.2300.230 as one half, one, two, and four times the decoded direction are removed. The logit difference likewise becomes more negative at every step, from −0.753-0.753 to −0.807-0.807, −0.859-0.859, −0.954-0.954, and −1.072-1.072.

Control directions do not produce the same monotonic deterioration. We compare this intervention with three controls evaluated by the same procedure. The shuffled-label control refits the same linear decoder after randomly permuting the repeated and non-repeated labels, which removes the relationship between the representation and the target label. The orthogonal control uses a random direction with its component along the decoded duplication direction projected out. We also evaluate five independently sampled random directions. Every direction, including the decoded one, is scaled to unit norm before removal, so the removal-strength multiplier means the same thing in every arm. Figure 25 plots the full sweep: the orthogonal, shuffled and random controls all leave floor behaviour approximately unchanged.

The decoded direction contains information that distinguishes repeated from non-repeated states, but removing it consistently worsens floor behaviour. It is therefore not the harmful causal quantity identified by the copying interventions. This result illustrates why linear decodability and causal importance must be evaluated separately.

F.3 Testing for an Additional Learned Routing Correction

The source-identity experiments show that attention heads copy name information from earlier positions. When the same name occurs at both S​1S1 and S​2S2, however, some attenuation of that copying can arise mechanically, because a fixed amount of attention is distributed across two occurrences of the same identity. We therefore ask whether native routing does anything measurably more protective than this passive effect.

For each copying head we construct a passive-split comparison. We preserve the total attention mass the head assigns to S​1S1 and S​2S2 but divide that mass equally between the two positions, leaving the value vectors unchanged. This creates a reference in which attention is redistributed between the two occurrences without introducing an additional content-dependent routing decision. Figure 23 shows the same attention mass before and after the split.

We then compare the native-routing effect with the passive-split effect on the three-name margin, item by item, and report the native effect minus the passive effect. Starting from the same-second-mention donor’s unmodified end-query attention row, we preserve its total mass on the two subject positions but divide that mass equally between them, leaving the rest of the row and the value vectors unchanged. We refer to the unmodified donor allocation as native routing and the equalised version as the passive split. Under this convention a negative value means native routing is more protective than the passive split, which is the direction expected if an additional learned routing computation is actively reducing harmful repeated-name copying.

Across the seven settings for which the comparison is available, every difference has magnitude below the analysis bound of 0.020.02. Six of the seven are positive, the opposite direction from the prediction above, and several of the template-aware intervals include zero. Table 8 gives all seven with both uncertainty procedures. The separately trained 160M setting has no passive-split arm and is not included. Figure 26 plots the seven paired differences.

We compare the paired native-minus-passive effect with an analysis bound of 0.02. Every available point estimate lies within this bound, although several template-aware intervals include values outside it. The result therefore constrains the measured difference to be small relative to this comparison value without establishing exact equivalence.

We therefore do not invoke an additional learned routing correction to explain the early attenuation. The account used in this paper requires repeated-name copying to be harmful at the floor and mature suppression to become important later. It does not require a separate early corrective router.

F.4 Results of the alternative-account tests

These controls constrain several alternative explanations for the floor behaviour. The repeated-name preference is inconsistent with the tested superadditive amplification account because the measured interaction has the opposite sign. A linearly decoded duplication direction is present, but removing it worsens rather than repairs the prediction. Native attention routing also provides no measurable protection beyond the passive split at the resolution of the comparison.

The positive evidence for copying remains the intervention evidence in Appendix D. Replacing the selected heads improves floor behaviour, and changing the identity supplied at their source changes the identity they support downstream. The resulting account requires harmful repeated-name copying at the floor and later development of mature suppression without requiring a separate early corrective router.

Appendix G Identifying and Tracing the Mature Suppressing Head

Section 5 follows one attention head backward through training at each model size. This appendix separates three operations that should not be conflated: selecting the head, characterising its native computation, and testing it causally.

G.1 Selection by mature replacement effect

At the mature checkpoint we evaluate every attention head individually. For a given head we replace its output vector with that head’s mean over the prompts and token positions of each sentence-template block, leaving the rest of the model unchanged, and measure the change in the I​OIO versus SS logit difference. The head whose replacement causes the largest decrease is selected. This returns L8H9 at 160M, L12H12 at 410M, and L11H0 at 1B.

The selection criterion is therefore behavioural and intervention-based. It asks which individual head makes the largest measured contribution to the mature model’s preference for the correct name over the repeated name.

The replacement used here differs from the copying intervention in Appendix D. That experiment constructs one fixed vector from separate non-repeated control prompts. Here each candidate head is replaced by its own mean over the prompts and token positions of each sentence-template block. We therefore call this mature-head mean replacement rather than control-mean replacement.

Because the replacement effect is used to select the head, the selected head’s large mature replacement effect is selection-conditioned. The later causal experiments, including the parameter transplant and the activation graft, test different quantities and provide independent evidence.

G.2 Native attention and direct output projection

After selecting the head we inspect its behaviour in the unmodified mature model. First we measure the share of its attention from END that falls on the second occurrence of the repeated name. Second we compute the direct projection of the head’s output at END onto that name’s unembedding direction, where a negative value means the head’s own output is aligned with lowering the repeated name.

These are descriptive attributions. They are not intervention effects and are not used to select the head.

At maturity the selected head at 160M places 0.9340.934 of its attention on the second mention with a direct output projection of −6.220-6.220. At 410M the values are 0.3360.336 and −2.105-2.105, and at 1B they are 0.5270.527 and −7.269-7.269. All three attend to the repeated mention and write in a direction that lowers it. This characterises what the selected heads do, and should not be presented as independent confirmation of the selection procedure.

G.3 Development across training

We trace the same mature-selected head backward through earlier checkpoints without reselecting at each step.

At 160M both properties are small around the floor. At step 512 the head places 0.0470.047 of its attention on the second mention with projection −0.005-0.005; at step 1000, 0.0210.021 and −0.016-0.016; and at the floor at step 2000, 0.0090.009 and −0.034-0.034. At step 3000, during behavioural recovery, these change sharply to 0.8490.849 and −1.338-1.338. At step 5000 they are 0.6920.692 and −4.590-4.590, and at maturity 0.9340.934 and −6.220-6.220.

The trajectory is not globally monotonic. Attention falls slightly across the earliest checkpoints, rises sharply around recovery, and changes again afterwards. The supported statement is therefore that the selected head is nearly inactive at the floor and becomes strongly engaged around recovery, not that either quantity increases monotonically throughout training.

The 410M trajectory shows the same broad separation between a weak floor state and a strongly engaged later state, and is likewise non-monotonic after recovery. At the floor attention is 0.0620.062 and the projection is −0.005-0.005; at step 3000 they are 0.7220.722 and −0.246-0.246; and at maturity 0.3360.336 and −2.105-2.105. For 1B only the floor and mature endpoints are available, with attention rising from 0.0140.014 to 0.5270.527. Figure 34 and Table 9 give the full trajectory. The projection changes from −0.025-0.025 to −7.269-7.269. That supports an endpoint contrast rather than a detailed trajectory.

G.4 Suppression develops around behavioural recovery

The backward trace shows that the computation associated with lowering the repeated name at maturity is weak at the floor and becomes strongly expressed around behavioural recovery. Attention and direct output projection describe the head’s native computation across training. Appendix H tests its causal importance through output replacement, activation grafting, and parameter transplantation.

Appendix H Causal Tests of the Mature Suppressing Head

This appendix asks whether the mature-selected head contributes to mature performance, whether its learned computation is sufficient to improve the floor, whether that improvement is specific, and how much of mature behaviour can be reconstructed when other helpful heads are added.

H.1 Contribution to mature behaviour

We first measure how much mature behaviour depends on the selected head, using the mature-head mean replacement defined above. At 160M the native mature logit difference is 3.7903.790; replacing L8H9 lowers it to 1.1311.131, a change of −2.659-2.659, while forced-choice accuracy remains 0.7770.777. At 410M it falls from 3.0933.093 to 1.3371.337, a change of −1.755-1.755, with accuracy 0.9000.900. At 1B it falls from 3.2263.226 to 1.6341.634, a change of −1.592-1.592, with accuracy 0.9930.993.

Replacing the selected head substantially weakens the mature preference while forced-choice accuracy remains above chance at all three sizes. The head is therefore an important part of the recovered computation, while other components also contribute.

H.2 Backward parameter transplantation

We next test whether what the head learns by maturity is sufficient to improve the floor. For each model we copy the mature head’s query, key, value, and output matrices into the same head at the floor checkpoint, together with the head-specific query, key, and value biases. The attention-layer output bias is shared across heads and is not transplanted. All other floor parameters remain unchanged.

The modified floor model then performs a normal forward pass and recomputes the transplanted head’s activations from its own inputs. This distinguishes parameter transplantation from activation grafting, in which a precomputed activation is inserted directly. Figure 28 shows what each operation moves and what the floor model then does with it.

The transplant produces a large partial rescue. At 160M the logit difference moves from −0.753-0.753 to +0.849+0.849 with accuracy 0.6870.687, closing 35.335.3 percent of the floor-to-mature gap. At 410M it moves from −0.702-0.702 to +1.876+1.876 with accuracy 0.8930.893, closing 67.967.9 percent. At 1B it moves from −0.543-0.543 to +0.984+0.984 with accuracy 0.8100.810, closing 40.540.5 percent.

The mature parameters are therefore sufficient to move every floor checkpoint from a negative to a positive logit difference. The rescue is substantial, incomplete, and varies across scale. It supports partial sufficiency, not the claim that one head reconstructs the entire mature computation. This is stronger than observing that the head’s attention or projection grows during training, because the transplant changes the early model’s behaviour by supplying later-learned parameters.

H.3 Specificity controls

Random parameter bundle.

The same parameter-copying operation is applied to a seeded bundle of eight heads, excluding the selected suppressing head and the twenty heads with the strongest direct contribution toward the correct name. The bundle closes −4.7-4.7 percent of the gap at 160M, 10.710.7 percent at 410M, and 5.95.9 percent at 1B, against 35.335.3, 67.967.9, and 40.540.5 percent for the single selected head.

This comparison favours the control in parameter count because the control receives eight heads while the treatment receives one. It shows that copying mature parameters into the floor is not generically sufficient to produce the observed rescue. It is not a head-for-head matched comparison and should not be described as one. Figure 35 compares the two transplants.

Output-norm-matched activation graft.

A separate experiment supplies the mature head’s activation rather than its parameters. For each prompt the mature activation of the selected head is inserted at the corresponding site in the floor model, so the floor model does not recompute the head from its own query, key, and value inputs. A control head whose output norm is closest to the suppressor’s is chosen, and the same operation is performed with it.

At 160M, grafting the suppressing head changes the logit difference by +0.583+0.583 against +0.013+0.013 for the output-norm-matched control head. At 410M the values are +0.752+0.752 and −0.351-0.351.

This is a one-for-one specificity control, but it answers a different causal question from parameter transplantation. The graft asks whether the mature head’s realised output on these prompts can improve the floor. The transplant asks whether the mature parameters can recompute a helpful output inside the early network. The two are convergent evidence rather than results to be pooled. Figure 32 plots both grafts.

H.4 Reconstruction with correct-name writers

The one-head transplant leaves part of the mature gap unclosed, which is expected because mature behaviour also depends on components that promote the correct name.

At 410M the selected head alone closes 67.967.9 percent of the gap. Adding the mature parameters of the strongest correct-name-writing heads cumulatively raises this to 88.188.1 percent with all eight writers added, at forced-choice accuracy 0.9330.933.

This supports a division of labour. Figure 29 plots the gap closed as writers are added.

The suppressing head removes support from the repeated competitor while correct-name writers promote the correct one, and the mature behaviour is therefore not reconstructed by the suppressor alone. This experiment is available at 410M and is not a three-scale result.

H.5 Output scaling leaves the floor below chance

One possible explanation of the transplant result is that the floor head already performs the mature operation but too weakly. If so, multiplying the floor head’s own output should improve behaviour. It does not.

At 160M, scaling the immature head’s output by two, four, eight, and sixteen moves the logit difference from −0.753-0.753 to −0.744-0.744, −0.720-0.720, −0.655-0.655, and −0.535-0.535, with accuracy moving from 0.3170.317 to 0.3630.363 at the largest factor. The floor remains below chance throughout. At 410M the corresponding sixteen-fold values are −0.590-0.590 and 0.3270.327, again below chance.

The floor head is therefore not a smaller version of the mature suppressing computation. Figure 30 gives the logit difference and accuracy at each multiplier.

The transplant supplies a change in what the head computes, including its routing and output transformation, rather than only an increase in magnitude.

H.6 The mature suppressing head contributes and partially rescues the floor

Four conclusions follow. The selected head makes a substantial contribution to the magnitude of mature correctness, but replacing it does not reproduce the floor. Its mature parameters are partially sufficient to rescue the floor at all three primary sizes. Both the eight-head parameter control and the matched one-head activation control show the rescue is not a generic consequence of importing mature components. And amplifying the immature version fails, so the critical developmental change concerns the head’s learned computation rather than its raw magnitude.

Together with the trajectory above, these results support a mature suppressing computation that is weak during the below-chance window, develops around recovery, and then contributes causally to the recovered behaviour.

Appendix I Distributed Upstream Dependence of the Suppressing Head

The mature suppressing head depends on an early feed-forward-block state, while the direct connection from that block to the head carries almost none of the measured dependence.

I.1 Early feed-forward-block replacement

For each prompt we construct a matched non-repeated control prompt on the same sentence template, run it, and cache the output of its first feed-forward block. We then run the original repeated-name prompt while replacing only that block’s output with the cached control activation. The original tokens are unchanged, so the repeated name remains present at the second mention and any downstream change comes from replacing the residual-stream activation rather than editing the input.

Across the tested early blocks, the first produces the largest behavioural change. Replacing its output with the matched non-repeated value substantially reduces the harmful floor preference and can bring forced-choice accuracy close to chance.

This identifies the first feed-forward block as an important early source of repetition-sensitive state. Because the intervention replaces the block’s complete output, it identifies the source of the causal effect without isolating a single feature within that state.

I.2 Dependence of the mature suppressing head

At maturity we apply the first-block replacement and then measure the selected head’s attention to the second mention. It decreases from 0.930.93 to 0.680.68 at 160M, from 0.340.34 to 0.160.16 at 410M, and from 0.530.53 to 0.280.28 at 1B.

The decrease occurs at all three sizes, showing that the mature suppressing head’s routing depends partly on information computed early in the network. The dependency is incomplete, since substantial attention remains after replacement. This supports a causal dependency from the early state into the mature head’s behaviour, but does not identify the route by which it is transmitted.

I.3 Isolating the direct route

A head’s query input contains the sum of many earlier residual contributions, so replacing the entire query input would conflate the first block’s contribution with every other upstream one.

To isolate only the direct route, we compute the difference between the first block’s output on the matched control and on the original prompt, and add only that difference to the suppressing head’s downstream input, leaving every other residual contribution unchanged. This edge-level intervention asks how much of the total first-block dependence reaches the head directly, without passing through intermediate components. Figure 33 separates the total first-block dependence from the isolated direct route.

Two shares are measured. On the head’s attention to the second mention, the direct route carries exactly 0.00.0 at all three sizes. On the final logit difference it carries 0.0600.060 percent at 160M, −0.013-0.013 percent at 410M, and 0.0090.009 percent at 1B. Both are effectively zero, and the small negative logit estimate at 410M should be read as estimation variation around zero rather than a meaningful negative route. We report both because the dependence described above is measured on attention while the routing literature more often reports a logit share, and the two agree here.

Because the head measurably depends on the first-block state while the isolated direct route carries approximately none of that dependence, the information must reach the head through intermediate computation.

I.4 Upstream dependence passes through intermediate computation

The experiments establish that replacing the first feed-forward block’s state changes floor behaviour, that the mature suppressing head partly depends on that state, and that the direct route from the block to the head carries approximately none of the measured dependence.

The appropriate conclusion is distributed upstream dependence rather than a single direct connection from the first feed-forward block to the suppressing head. Intermediate attention heads, feed-forward blocks, and residual-stream paths may all contribute, but this appendix does not assign the dependence to a particular sequence.

Appendix J Extensions Across Scale and Model Family

The detailed copying-to-suppression account is established on the released Pythia 160M, 410M, and 1B models. This appendix examines which parts of that account extend to additional Pythia sizes and to independently trained GPT-2 and OLMo models.

The interventions differ across the settings below. We therefore interpret the sign and timing within each experiment rather than comparing effect magnitudes across settings.

J.1 Additional Pythia sizes

J.1.1 First feed-forward block replacement across five sizes

For each prompt we construct a matched control on the same sentence template with the same correct name, in which the second occurrence of the repeated name is replaced by a different name so that no name appears twice. We run the model on the control prompt and cache the output of the first transformer block’s feed-forward module, then run the original repeated-name prompt while replacing that module output with the cached control activation. The evaluated prompt’s tokens are unchanged, so this is an internal activation replacement rather than an input edit. Figure 36 follows the cached activation from the control run into the target run.

Table 10 gives the change at each size, and replacing an early activation with its non-repeated counterpart improves floor behaviour across the whole range. The effect is much smaller at 410M than elsewhere, and we retain that heterogeneity rather than presenting the result as a uniform scaling law.

Across these five sizes, the first feed-forward block carries repetition-sensitive information that harms the floor prediction. The detailed head-level copying analysis is evaluated separately in the three primary models.

J.1.2 Pythia 2.8B

We report two distinct interventions at this size and keep their interpretations separate.

Input edit.

The second occurrence of the repeated name is replaced directly in the token sequence by a third name. At the floor the unmodified model has forced-choice accuracy 0.2970.297 and logit difference −0.504-0.504, and this edit improves the logit difference by +0.456+0.456. At maturity the same edit changes it by −4.076-4.076, so input-level sensitivity to repetition reverses between the floor and maturity.

Early feed-forward activation replacement.

A separate experiment replaces the outputs of the early feed-forward blocks while leaving the prompt tokens unchanged. Resampling those activations from matched non-repeated prompts raises floor accuracy from 0.2970.297 to 0.6030.603. Replacing the same activations with their mean instead gives 0.4670.467. The replacement distribution therefore matters, and we report the two separately rather than treating feed-forward replacement as a single intervention.

At 2.8B, both the token edit and the internal activation replacements show harmful early sensitivity to the repeated relation. The input-edit effect additionally reverses at maturity.

J.2 Independently trained GPT-2 models

We evaluate two independently trained GPT-2 Small models released by the Stanford CRFM Mistral project (Karamcheti et al., 2021), alias-gpt2-small-x21 and battlestar-gpt2-small-x49. For consistency with the paper-wide convention, all intervention effects in this subsection are reported as replaced minus native.

The mature-defined suppressing head is L10H10 in the first run and L10H7 in the second. Each is fixed at the mature checkpoint by its replacement effect and then traced backward through training. Their differing identities already indicate that the developmental role is more stable than the component implementing it.

We apply two interventions. The first replaces the output of the first feed-forward block with the corresponding output from a matched non-repeated prompt, following the procedure above. The second applies mature-head mean replacement to the head that later becomes the mature suppressor, measuring how much the model at each checkpoint depends on that future component.

At step 1500 the first run has native logit difference −1.475-1.475, and the early activation replacement changes it by +1.123+1.123 while replacing the future suppressor changes it by about −0.002-0.002. The second run has native logit difference −1.741-1.741, with corresponding values of +1.472+1.472 and about −0.002-0.002.

At maturity both interventions reverse. The early activation replacement changes the logit difference by −4.081-4.081 and −4.607-4.607 in the two runs. Replacing the mature suppressing head changes it by −1.928-1.928 and −1.506-1.506, lowering the mature logit difference from 3.4083.408 to 1.4801.480 and from 3.6473.647 to 2.1422.142. Every value quoted here is the effect of the intervention, so a negative number means the replacement moved the model away from the correct name and the native component was therefore helping.

The common result is an ordering. Repetition-sensitive early computation is already causally important at the poor checkpoint, the head that later performs substantial suppression is nearly inert there, and that component becomes important later. The suppressor identity and the detailed timing differ between the two runs, so the developmental ordering recurs more robustly than the identity of the implementing head.

J.3 OLMo-1B

We evaluate OLMo-1B (Groeneveld et al., 2024) at the early revision step1000-tokens4B and at the released final revision. At the early checkpoint forced-choice accuracy is 0.4370.437 and the logit difference is −0.220-0.220. At maturity accuracy is 1.0001.000 and the logit difference is 4.4254.425.

For each prompt we construct a matched non-repeated control on the same sentence template and replace the residual-stream activation at the second occurrence of the repeated name with the corresponding activation from that control, across layers 4 to 7. The prompt tokens and all activations outside the selected position and layer band remain native.

At the early checkpoint the replacement improves the logit difference by +0.0448+0.0448 with interval [+0.0349,+0.0549][+0.0349,+0.0549]. At maturity the same intervention changes it by −5.137-5.137 with interval [−5.257,−5.018][-5.257,-5.018]. The causal role of the second-mention residual state therefore reverses between the two evaluated checkpoints.

The state-level developmental reversal therefore extends beyond Pythia and GPT-2. This experiment evaluates the changing causal role of the second-mention state in OLMo, while the full head-level copying account is evaluated in the primary Pythia models.

J.4 Cross-scale and cross-family summary

The extensions above support a recurring developmental motif without implying one universal circuit. Across additional Pythia sizes, disrupting repetition-sensitive early computation improves behaviour at the floor. In two independently trained GPT-2 models that early computation is already causally important while the future mature suppressor remains nearly inert. In OLMo the causal role of the second-mention residual state reverses between an early and a mature checkpoint.

The strongest copying-specific evidence remains the donor-free ensemble replacement and the source-identity intervention on the primary models. The additional settings each establish a subset of the account without showing that the same heads or the same intervention-defined mechanism recur everywhere. Table 11 summarises every setting.

Appendix K Extensions Across Tasks

The main analysis concerns the naming task. We next examine whether related developmental patterns appear on other structured prediction tasks. Figure 37 illustrates the subject-verb agreement and factual-recall prompts. Each task uses its own score and intervention, allowing us to compare developmental timing without assuming that the same circuit implements every result.

K.1 Greater-Than

K.1.1 Task and score

Each prompt describes an event spanning two years and ends partway through the closing year, for example “The war lasted from the year 1723 to the year 17”. A plausible continuation completes the century with a two-digit value greater than 23.

Writing Y​YYY for the final two digits of the starting year, we define

GT=∑v>Y​Yp⁡(v)−∑v≤Y​Yp⁡(v),\mathrm{GT}=\sum_{v>YY}p(v)-\sum_{v\leq YY}p(v), (4)

where vv ranges over the valid two-digit continuation tokens. A positive score means the model assigns more probability to continuations representing a later year. Forced-choice accuracy is the fraction of prompts with a positive score, so chance is one half.

We use only starting years for which the year tokenises into an unambiguous century token followed by a two-digit token. The Y​YYY position is located directly in each tokenised prompt rather than inferred from a fixed offset.

K.1.2 Matched-state intervention

For every target prompt we construct a matched prompt with the same event description and a different starting year, so the two differ only in the year. We replace the residual-stream activation at the target’s Y​YYY token with the corresponding activation from the matched prompt across an early layer band, and the rest of the forward pass proceeds normally.

At step 1000 the change in the score is +0.082+0.082 at 160M with interval [0.017,0.148][0.017,0.148], +0.097+0.097 at 410M with [0.036,0.158][0.036,0.158], and +0.319+0.319 at 1B with [0.285,0.356][0.285,0.356]. At maturity the same intervention changes the score by −0.737-0.737 with [−0.824,−0.651][-0.824,-0.651], −0.667-0.667 with [−0.747,−0.588][-0.747,-0.588], and −0.733-0.733 with [−0.819,−0.648][-0.819,-0.648]. The intervention effect therefore reverses sign across training at all three sizes.

At 160M and 1B the early behavioural score is also below chance, at 0.3200.320 and 0.2670.267. At 410M early accuracy is already 0.5530.553. The 410M result is therefore a causal reversal in the role of the year state without a corresponding below-chance behavioural window. The Greater-Than experiment therefore shows that the causal contribution of a task-relevant state can reverse during training. Such a reversal can occur whether or not the early behavioural score falls below chance.

K.2 Subject-verb agreement

This task asks the model to prefer the verb form agreeing with the grammatical subject even when an opposite-number attractor noun appears between the subject and the verb. The intervention replaces the residual-stream activation at that attractor noun with the corresponding activation from a matched control prompt.

The result does not follow the developmental pattern studied in this paper. The effect is positive at every evaluated checkpoint, moving from +0.020+0.020 with interval [0.018,0.023][0.018,0.023] at step 256 to +0.022+0.022 with [0.017,0.028][0.017,0.028] at maturity. There is no sign reversal and the effect remains small throughout training.

Subject-verb agreement therefore provides a contrasting case in which the tested intervention remains small and positive throughout training. Changing causal roles are not automatic across structured linguistic tasks.

K.3 Factual recall with a competing entity

Each prompt introduces two entities and asks for a property of one of them, so the more recently mentioned but incorrect entity competes with the correct answer. The behavioural score is the correct entity’s logit minus the competing entity’s logit, and forced-choice accuracy is the fraction of prompts for which this is positive.

Across training, accuracy changes from 0.5670.567 at step 512 to 0.0830.083 at step 3000 and then recovers to 0.9170.917 at maturity, so this task exhibits a pronounced behavioural dip of its own.

We identify a task-specific head from the mature checkpoint that contributes to lowering the competing entity, and trace that same head backward through training. Mature-head mean replacement changes the score by −0.029-0.029 at step 2000 and +0.044+0.044 at step 3000, both close to zero. At maturity, replacement changes the score by −1.330-1.330 from a native score of 1.9701.970, meaning the native head contributes substantially to the mature preference.

This provides evidence for a developmental pattern in which a mature suppressing component remains weak during poor intermediate behaviour and becomes substantial during recovery. The copying-specific interventions used for the naming task were not run on factual recall.

K.4 Cross-task summary

Across the additional tasks the evidence is deliberately uneven. Greater-Than shows a clear causal sign reversal in the role of an early token state at all three model sizes, although only two of them also fall below chance. Factual recall shows a deep behavioural dip accompanied by a mature-defined suppressing component that remains weak until later in training. Subject-verb agreement provides a negative case in which the tested intervention remains small and positive throughout.

These results show that temporary developmental failures and early-to-late changes in causal role are not unique to the naming task. Table 12 summarises the four tasks, and the full copying-specific account remains restricted to the three primary Pythia models.

Appendix L Training From Scratch and Ordinary-Text Controls

This appendix uses three complementary training experiments to examine how the developmental phenomenon can arise.

Controlled task injection tests how the frequency of structured task examples affects learning and generalisation. A minimal symbolic task tests whether a copy-heavy distribution with a rarer override rule is sufficient to produce a dip and intervention reversal. Models trained only on ordinary text test whether harmful repetition sensitivity can appear without explicit task injection. Each experiment addresses a different part of the training account.

L.1 Controlled task injection

L.1.1 Model and training setup

We train an eight-layer GPT-2-style transformer with eight attention heads, model dimension 512, and a context length of 256 tokens. The feed-forward width is left at the library default of four times the model dimension, giving 2048.

Training uses AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, weight decay 0.010.01, betas 0.90.9 and 0.950.95, batch size 32, a linear warmup over the first 1000 steps, and a cosine decay to one tenth of the peak learning rate, for 40000 steps in total.

The ordinary-text component is drawn from WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2017). At each batch position an ordinary-text sequence is replaced by a task-structured sequence with probability equal to the injection rate, and the four rates are 00, 0.050.05, 0.150.15, and 0.300.30. The task pool contains 4000 preconstructed sequences assembled from eight sentence frames, twelve place words, and twelve object words. In the principal comparison the four conditions share the same parameter initialisation and the same ordinary-text stream, so the injection rate is the intended difference between them. Additional independently seeded runs test whether the qualitative trajectories persist under broader training randomness, including model initialisation and the sampling of both the ordinary text and the injected task rows.

L.1.2 Held-out and in-distribution evaluations

The sentence frames are shared between training and evaluation because they define the task structure. The names are not. Injected sequences draw from one name pool while the held-out evaluation uses a disjoint pool.

Each checkpoint is evaluated on a held-out set of 300 prompts using names absent from the injected sequences, and on an in-distribution set of 300 prompts using names from the injection pool. The held-out set measures whether the learned rule generalises to unseen names. The in-distribution set distinguishes a failure to generalise from a failure to learn the injected task at all. A model may therefore reach ceiling in distribution while remaining substantially below ceiling on held-out names. Figure 38 shows the training mixture and the two evaluations it feeds.

L.1.3 Results

With no task injection the model does not acquire the override rule, ending at held-out accuracy 0.2830.283 and in-distribution accuracy 0.2170.217.

At injection rate 0.050.05 held-out accuracy falls to 0.4570.457 at step 2000 before recovering to 0.9030.903, with in-distribution accuracy reaching 1.0001.000. At rate 0.150.15 the principal run reaches a minimum of 0.4670.467 and recovers to 0.9100.910, again reaching 1.0001.000 in distribution. At rate 0.300.30 held-out accuracy does not fall below its starting value and ends at 0.7570.757, while in-distribution accuracy reaches 1.0001.000. At rates 0.050.05 and 0.150.15 the temporary below-chance point followed by recovery appears across all three training seeds, whereas the zero-injection models remain below chance and the 0.300.30 condition is already above chance by the first post-initial evaluation. Figure 39 shows all three trajectories for each rate.

Intermediate injection rates therefore produce both the clearest temporary deterioration and the strongest held-out generalisation. Zero injection produces no task learning, while the highest rate permits ceiling in-distribution performance but weaker transfer to unseen names. Figure 40 plots both evaluations. The relationship between injection rate and held-out behaviour is non-monotonic.

Within this training setup, the temporary dip depends on the frequency of task-structured examples and is not an unavoidable consequence of eventually learning the task. The intermediate injection rates produce the clearest temporary deterioration and the strongest held-out generalisation.

L.2 A minimal symbolic task

L.2.1 Task

We construct a minimal task that retains the competition between ordinary copying and a rarer override rule while removing natural-language structure. Each sequence contains three symbols drawn from a vocabulary of size VV. An ordinary copy example contains three distinct symbols and targets the final symbol,

[x,y,z]→z,[x,\,y,\,z]\rightarrow z,

while an override example repeats the first symbol in third position but targets the middle symbol,

[a,b,a]→b.[a,\,b,\,a]\rightarrow b.

A model that has learned only the ordinary copying rule succeeds on copy examples but systematically predicts the repeated final symbol on override examples. This is a minimal analogue of the competition studied in the rest of the paper, not the task itself. Here copying refers only to the behavioural rule of predicting the final input symbol. It is not intended to reproduce the attention-head copying mechanism identified in the Pythia models. Chance accuracy on override examples is 1/V1/V rather than one half, because the prediction is made over the full candidate-symbol vocabulary.

L.2.2 Models and training sweep

The models are two-layer transformers with four attention heads. We vary the model dimension over {16,32,64}\{16,32,64\} with the feed-forward width fixed at twice that, the vocabulary size over {50,100}\{50,100\}, the learning rate over {3×10−5,10−4,3×10−4}\{3\times 10^{-5},10^{-4},3\times 10^{-4}\}, the training length over 30000 or 50000 steps, and the copy-example fraction over {0.90,0.95,0.98}\{0.90,0.95,0.98\}. The remainder of each batch consists of override examples, and we refer to the copy-example fraction as copy pressure. The large number of possible symbol combinations prevents the task from reducing to memorisation of a small fixed list of override triples.

L.2.3 Intervention and criteria

At each evaluated checkpoint we substitute the token at the repeated position. For every example a replacement symbol is drawn uniformly from the vocabulary excluding both the repeated symbol and the override target, and its embedding, together with the position embedding for that slot, replaces the original. The substitution is therefore an independent per-example change of symbol identity at the input embedding rather than a random continuous vector, and no norm matching is applied. We then measure the change in the logit difference between the override target and the repeated symbol.

A positive effect means that disrupting the repeated position improves the preference for the override target, and a negative effect means the same disruption harms it.

We apply two trajectory criteria. A behavioural dip occurs when the lowest evaluated override accuracy after the initial checkpoint falls below chance. An intervention reversal occurs when the measured effect is above +0.1+0.1 at one evaluated checkpoint and below −0.1-0.1 at the next evaluated checkpoint, which is how the criterion is implemented.

L.2.4 Results

Ten runs are evaluated. Eight vary vocabulary size, model dimension, learning rate, training duration, and copy pressure. Two further runs repeat the strongest configuration under new seeds, giving three seeds for that configuration in total.

All ten runs exhibit a behavioural dip, and nine of the ten exhibit the intervention reversal. Figure 41 counts the runs meeting each criterion. Together, these runs provide a controlled sufficiency result: a training distribution dominated by an ordinary copying rule but containing a rarer override rule can produce both temporary below-chance behaviour and a reversal in the causal role of the repeated-position state. The experiment establishes this result at the level of the training distribution, while its internal mechanism and relationship to natural-language pretraining remain open.

L.3 Models trained only on ordinary text

L.3.1 Setup

The controlled-injection experiments deliberately add task-structured sequences. We therefore perform a separate test using two small language models trained by the authors on ordinary web text with no task-specific sequences added.

Both are GPT-2 architecture models with eight layers, model dimension 512, and eight attention heads, using the GPT-2 tokenizer and its vocabulary of 50257, trained on a stream of OpenWebText at learning rate 6×10−46\times 10^{-4}. The two runs differ in length: the first was trained to step 200000 and yields 65 evaluated checkpoints, the second to step 105000 and yields 46.

At every checkpoint we evaluate the same repeated-name task on a fixed set of 200 prompts. We also construct a matched control prompt in which the second occurrence of the repeated name is replaced by a third single-token name. The evaluated prompt itself remains unchanged. Instead, across an early-to-middle band of transformer blocks running from one quarter to one half of the depth, we replace its hidden state at the second mention with the corresponding state produced by the control prompt, and measure the resulting change in logit difference. This hidden-state replacement leaves the evaluated tokens unchanged and intervenes only on the internal state at the second mention.

L.3.2 Behavioural trajectory

Both models remain close to chance in the two-name comparison, but their mean logit difference becomes negative over substantial portions of training. The first run reaches −0.260-0.260 at step 25000 and the second reaches −0.259-0.259 at step 40000. The first ends at +0.141+0.141 and the second at −0.231-0.231, so neither develops the strong recovered preference seen in mature Pythia.

The replacement improves the logit difference at 64 of the 65 evaluated checkpoints in the first run and at all 46 in the second. This establishes that a repetition-sensitive preference against the correct name can emerge during ordinary-text training without explicit injection of the evaluation task. Figure 42 plots both runs.

These runs show that harmful repetition sensitivity can emerge during ordinary-text training without explicit task injection. Because neither model develops a strong recovered preference, they capture the harmful early side of the pattern without its later corrective phase.

L.4 Complementary evidence from three training settings

The three experiments provide complementary evidence.

Controlled task injection shows that the presence and depth of temporary deterioration depend on the frequency of task-structured examples, and that ceiling performance on familiar names does not imply equivalent generalisation to unseen names.

The minimal symbolic task gives a sufficiency result. A common copying rule combined with a rarer override rule can produce both a behavioural dip and a causal reversal in models trained from scratch.

The ordinary-text runs show that harmful repetition sensitivity can emerge without explicit task injection. Because those models never reach a strong recovered state, they do not establish that ordinary web-text training alone reproduces the complete copying-to-suppression trajectory.

These experiments make the developmental phenomenon easier to reproduce and constrain possible explanations for it. Determining why the natural Pythia training distribution learns harmful copying before mature suppression remains an open training-dynamics question.

Appendix M Earlier Version and Reproducibility

M.1 Relationship to the Workshop Version

A preliminary version of this work reported the initial training-time sign flip (Dahiya and Blondin, 2026). This paper develops the causal account and expands the evaluation across interventions, controls, model scales, model families, and training settings.

M.2 Released Artefacts

The code and results supporting this paper are available at https://github.com/Tejas7007/EMNLP_Findings_2026_Copying_Before_Suppression, and the separately trained Pythia-160M model with its dense checkpoints through the early training transition is available at https://huggingface.co/teys7007/pythia-160m-seed42-dense (DOI: 10.57967/hf/10155).
